extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, novelists, and students of English literature
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical principles for judging novels and narrative art, especially character-portrayal, dialogue, plot-construction, and style in late-18th / early-19th-century English fiction. Emphasises distinctions between caricature/humours and subtle characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibition of human passions and whims (strength of novelist)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's chief strength is in the exhibition of human passions and whims: she is 'a character-monger' whose power lies in portraying human passions and whims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value writers who can exhibit human passions and eccentricities vividly; this quality is a primary merit even if other aspects (plot, style) are weaker. Example: Madame D'Arblay's strength lies in exhibiting human passions and whims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of caricature; seizing delicate lineaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Highest merit lies in seizing peculiarities which do not amount to deformity; the finest artists capture delicate lineaments and shades that distinguish two similar persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize subtle, discriminating touches that differentiate characters without overcharging a single trait. Examples: Garrick could seize slight differences of manner; contrast with Foote (caricature). A limner who can catch such slight peculiarities ranks highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of mixed, balanced passions (no single ruling passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters of the highest order are not governed by one ruling passion but by a 'mixed government' of many competing propensities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing characters to one dominant trait; portray multiple, interacting motives as Shakespeare does (e.g., Shylock's hate is mixed with pride, covetousness, religious feeling). This complexity gives a vivid, realistic portrait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparing use of humours/monomanias
rubrics_metrics.description: Humours (single morbid propensities) exist and can be imitated, but because they are rare in real life they 'ought... to be sparingly introduced' into realistic works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using humours can be effective and may yield memorable comic or grotesque figures, but over-reliance (making most characters monomaniacs) is a fault. The essay criticises Madame D'Arblay for leaving 'scarcely anything but humours.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness among commonplace characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Even commonplace or similar social types should be perfectly discriminated from each other by delicate touches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should make members of the same social group recognizably distinct (example: Jane Austen’s four clergymen are all of the same class yet clearly different). Achieve this through nuanced detail in speech and manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue as the medium for exhibiting human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue is a chief means of exhibiting human nature, capable of producing impressions as vivid as real-life acquaintance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well the dialogue renders character and variety of mind; Shakespeare is held up as the master for representing human nature 'by means of dialogue.' Look for dialogue that gives each character a distinctive voice and reveals mixed motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-consistent speech/jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should 'talk his own peculiar jargon'—each person must have a distinctive mode of speech appropriate to their temperament and rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether characters' speech habits and idioms are consistent and differentiating (the essay praises D'Arblay's success in producing peculiar jargons even when individual speeches may be monotonous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot-probability versus functional plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots should be probable in themselves, but improbable or 'rudely constructed' plots may be tolerable if they are 'admirably framed' to exhibit striking groups of eccentric characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge plots both on intrinsic probability and on how well they serve the author's artistic purpose. The critic allows improbabilities when the purpose is to assemble and display character contrasts, but marks implausible plotting as a weakness when it undermines the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between comedy/farce and genuine pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Success in comedy (even bordering on farce) is a merit; authors may also occasionally attain true pathos via 'exquisite strokes of natural tenderness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether comic exaggeration serves the work without collapsing into mere farce, and whether the author can achieve authentic pathetic moments (examples: Mrs. Hill’s account of her child's death; the parting scene in Camilla).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall variety and avoidance of monotony
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual characters’ talk is monotonous, the general effect should be a lively and agreeable diversity arising from the contrast of many humours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the ensemble effect: does the variety of humours and oppositions create sustained interest despite occasional monotony in separate voices?

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative and descriptive quality (historical/diary value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellent narrative and description can have historical value equal to diaries like Pepys's or Evelyn's; the account of the King's illness is cited as 'much excellent narrative and description.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and credit passages where narrative detail and descriptive power contribute documentary or discursive worth beyond fictional merit (useful to historians, illuminating character).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and purity of style; avoid ill-suited imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Style should be easy, clear, and free from offensive faults; authors should avoid imitating incongruous phraseology (e.g., Johnson) inappropriate to a tale of fashionable life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the writer's diction and phrasing suit the genre and tone. Imitating a great writer's manner (like Johnson) may be a mistake if that phraseology is out of place in fiction; look for grace, purity, and suiting of style to subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustaining mature powers; avoiding later degeneration of style
rubrics_metrics.description: An author ought not to undergo a 'pernicious change' in style as they mature; later works should not show a 'perversion of power' or loss of grace and purity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an author's later output for decline or change in tone/quality; the critic notes Madame D'Arblay's fall-off in grace and purity and considers this a serious reproach to her late fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of characterization and theatrical grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may assemble improbable meetings if those contrivances produce an 'exquisitely ludicrous effect' by bringing together contrasting humours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept contrivance as a dramaturgical tool when it creates comic or illustrative effects; but weigh this against the loss of credibility. Example: grouping four old fools to produce ludicrous conflict is permissible if artistically effective.
